paragraphs.text: JARID2-related neurodevelopmental syndrome is caused by JARID2 haploinsufficiency. It features developmental delay and cognitive impairment that ranges from borderline intellectual functioning to severe intellectual disability. Patients may also have hypotonia, gait disturbance, autistic features and behavior abnormalities. The facial features include a high anterior hairline, broad forehead, prominent supraorbital ridges, deeply set eyes, infraorbital dark circles, midface hypoplasia, depressed nasal bridge, bulbous nasal tip and full lips (Barøy et al., 2013; Verberne et al., 2022).

paragraphs.text: Barøy et al. (2013) reported 4 unrelated patients with de novo 6p22.3 deletions that included JARID2. Patient 1 was a 15-year-old Norwegian girl born to nonconsanguineous healthy parents. She had global developmental delay and moderate intellectual disability (IQ 35-49). She walked at 3.5 years and had severe expressive language delay. Other findings were periventricular white matter changes, syncope episodes suspected to be seizures, hyperactivity, sleeping difficulties, dyspraxia and an unsteady, broad-based gait. Skeletal findings included pes planovalgus, short metacarpals and first metatarsals, kyphosis and fifth-finger clinodactyly. Her face showed prominent supraorbital ridges, deep-set eyes, infraorbital dark circles, midface hypoplasia, hypotelorism, strabismus and a bulbous nasal tip. Her muscle tone was normal. Patient 2 was a 4-year-old boy born to nonconsanguineous healthy Norwegian and English parents. He had moderate intellectual disability, delayed eye contact, severe language delay, repetitive behavior and syncope episodes suspected to be seizures. He also had an atrial septal defect that closed spontaneously. His gait was broad-based and unsteady, and he seemed unable to stand on one leg at a time. He had the same facial features as patient 1, along with pes planovalgus and syndactyly of toes 2 to 4. His cerebral MRI was normal.

paragraphs.text: Patient 3 of Barøy et al. (2013) was a 6.5-year-old girl born to nonconsanguineous healthy Norwegian parents. In the neonatal period she had hypotonia, an umbilical hernia and apnea with cyanosis. Testing with the Bayley II at 5 years 10 months showed cognitive function corresponding to 12 to 13 months, suggesting severe intellectual disability (IQ 20-34). Evaluation with the ADOS showed behavior consistent with autism spectrum disorder. She also had severe language delay, hyperactivity, an unsteady gait and sleeping difficulties. Her face showed prominent supraorbital ridges, deep-set eyes, hypertelorism and midface hypoplasia, and her frontal teeth were irregularly placed. Patient 4 was a 6.5-year-old boy born to nonconsanguineous Lebanese parents. He had early-onset muscular hypotonia. Testing with the WPPSI-III at 6.5 years gave a borderline IQ of 74. He had language delay, dyspraxia, balance and coordination problems and gait disturbance. His facial features were prominent supraorbital ridges, deep-set eyes, infraorbital dark circles, midface hypoplasia, strabismus, a bulbous nasal tip, a short philtrum, full lips and a pointed chin. He also had syndactyly of toes 2 and 3, a sandal gap and fifth-finger clinodactyly. His cerebral MRI and EEG were normal. On photographs of 7 of 10 previously published patients with deletions that contained JARID2, the authors confirmed the same facial pattern. Impaired balance or coordination and/or gait disturbance had been noted in 4 of those 10 patients.

paragraphs.text: Verberne et al. (2022) reported 11 patients with JARID2 variants. Patient 1 was a 14-year-old boy with mild intellectual disability (IQ 61-74), autistic features, a broad forehead, infraorbital dark circles, pes planovalgus and mild hypermetropia, without hypotonia. Patient 2 was a 21-year-old woman with borderline intellectual functioning (IQ 82) and behavior abnormalities. She had a high anterior hairline, deeply set eyes, midface hypoplasia, a short philtrum, a submucous cleft palate and a bifid uvula. Patient 3 was an 18-year-old woman with mild intellectual disability (IQ 50) and autistic features. Her facial features were a high anterior hairline, deeply set eyes, infraorbital dark circles, a depressed nasal bridge, a bulbous nasal tip, a short philtrum and full lips. She also had fetal finger pads and slight bilateral tapering of digits II and V. Patient 4 was a 14-year-old boy with moderate intellectual disability, behavior abnormalities and autism spectrum disorder. He had a small posterior fossa cyst or mega cisterna magna, a high anterior hairline, a short philtrum, full lips and 2 cafe-au-lait macules. Patient 5 was a 5-year-old boy with developmental delay, hypotonia, an arachnoid cyst, a broad forehead, deeply set eyes, right cryptorchidism and congenital torticollis.

It had been inherited from a healthy parent, and its gene content did not appear relevant to the clinical presentation. A fifth patient had a de novo 116- to 163-kb deletion that included GMPR and part of ATXN1 but not JARID2. She had mild intellectual disability without dysmorphic features.

Given their nonspecific phenotypes and the absence of characteristic facial features, the authors suggested that these missense variants might very well be benign. They noted, however, that a negative episignature result does not rule out pathogenicity.
